title: Prepare the GC2 project presentation

summary: Presenting Team 17's Flickpond project: course requirements, design, evidence, demo rehearsal, facts to confirm.
opening_answer: We separated an inherited video app into Media and Processing behind contracts, with one Aurora cluster per service, a Publisher client, a Lambda short-encode lane and independently operated cloud workers. sections.title: A short opening that tells the truth

blocks.text: **30 seconds:** “Small teams need uploads turned into playable video without managing conversion. We built on an earlier Flickpond app: separate Media and Processing responsibilities, an API-based Publisher client and independently controlled cloud workers. We'll show the journey, the design, and what our measurements did and did not prove.”

**Two minutes:** Maya and Arun are content owners, Jules an integrator, Sam an operator (fictional personas). Media owns identity and asset access; Processing owns attempts and encoding. The Publisher CLI uses published contracts only.

**Headline with its boundary:** AWS V1 six-clip run: 1.449× at two workers (target 1.6×, missed), 2.347× at three (2.1×, met); 30-clip run not done. Short lane (`sl1021`): queue wait met, end-to-end 20 s not.

blocks.text: Top-down: scope, logical design, deployed evidence. The 8+2 demo is official; speaker hand-offs are recommendations.

sections.title: Tell one story through the four personas

blocks.text: Maya signs in to the Publisher CLI, submits a prepared folder of her recordings, gets one result per file, then plays a completed item (MP4, or HLS if present). Not student publishing: no shared classroom account or LMS. Arun is the browser story: upload, progress, owner-only playback.

Jules: the CLI calls the published API, no service import or database credential. Sam: capacity and Processing releases change separately from Media, shown by recorded evidence and version identities; no autoscaler or dashboard.

sections.title: Show the design, then name the evidence boundary

blocks.text: **Logical.** Media owns accounts, assets, upload identity and owner reads; Processing owns jobs, attempts, leases and encoding. SQL outbox/inbox makes publication recoverable with idempotent duplicates. The gateway passes trusted owner identity, so Processing never accepts a forged owner header.

**Physical (dc2-live).** API Gateway, Lambda, SQS, S3, CloudFront; short encodes on Lambda, others on finite Fargate. **Each service has its own Aurora cluster** (AD-29): isolated capacity and failure, but one region, not HA.

spec.title: Security scanning to the Security tab

blocks.text: **Lifecycle.** Change, tests, CI, image checks, admission, promotion, smoke. The gate stops fixable HIGH/CRITICAL findings only; AD-28 also scans the retained rollback image without bypassing the gate. Accepted unfixed: CVE-2025-52290 (ffmpeg, no Debian 13 fix; no inbound network). 22 October: 12 High CodeQL alerts (test, proof, dev-script code) dismissed; open: ZAP low/info on OpenAPI pages.

sections.title: Questions to expect and facts to confirm

blocks.a: Media owns identity and assets; Processing owns jobs and attempts. Separate contracts allow independent capacity and releases, at the cost of more messaging.

blocks.q: Does the platform prove the scalability target?
blocks.a: Partly. AWS V1 six clips: 2.347× at three workers (target 2.1×, met), 1.449× at two (1.6×, missed); no 30-clip run; the fixed-cap-3 V2-live run is no comparison.
No proof. One region; single-instance Aurora clusters isolate capacity and failure between services but give no replica failover. Claim no regional or database HA.

blocks.q: Why one Aurora cluster per service, and how was it done?
blocks.a: A shared cluster shared capacity and failure despite separate roles (AD-29). Media kept the original; Processing got a copy-on-write clone; each dropped the other's database; both pause at 0 ACU. Rehearsed on a throwaway stack, snapshot kept, CD run 39644028238. Cost: a second cluster's storage and wake.

blocks.q: What is the Lambda short lane, and what did it fix?
blocks.a: Clips ≤60 s, ≤64 MiB, ≤1080p go to a Lambda container (3008 MB, 900 s, concurrency 2); others to finite Fargate (cap 3). It removed the queue wait (0.26 s vs 32.6 s; $0.0003 vs $0.0021 per encode; 0 failures, table above) but 35–80 s per job is unexplained, so 20 s is still missed.

blocks.q: How is security checked, and what is left open?
blocks.a: CodeQL, Trivy per image, ZAP authenticated DAST, Ruff security, gitleaks; SARIF to code scanning, Dependabot on. 22 October: 12 High CodeQL alerts dismissed with reasons. Open: ZAP low/info on OpenAPI pages; accepted CVE-2025-52290 (ffmpeg).

blocks.q: What did Team 17 inherit, and what did it add?
blocks.a: Inherited: FFmpeg processing, HLS, worker replicas, basic CI. Added: Media/Processing split, contracts, Publisher, AWS platform and pipeline, Lambda short lane, per-service databases, security boundaries, experiments.

blocks.q: How much did each person work, and who authored each design?
blocks.a: The ledger allocates 33 person-days / 264 hours equally: 11 days / 88 hours each (8 h/day). Not timesheets; each person confirms; do not infer authorship from commits or agent activity. Project 1 membership statements have a provenance tension.

AISS-01..05. **01** performance misses (20 s end-to-end on both lanes, about 37 s long-clip queue wait, two-worker 1.449×, no 30-clip run). **02** public `execute-api` URL reachable beyond CloudFront, no WAF. **03** image-only rollback; schema never restored. **04** operations: broad CD role, no staging or reviewer gate, 13 alarms notify nobody, 7-day logs. **05** not established: lost-queue-entry timing, duplicate-output check after worker kill, restore drill, Publisher effort, actual spend.
